title: Live: Pretti Family Blames Federal Government for Shielding Alex’s Killers, Sparks Outcry
body:
The Pretti family has taken to the national stage, accusing the federal government of protecting the agents who killed their son, Alex Pretti, during a 2024 immigration enforcement operation. In a televised press conference held yesterday, Michael and Susan Pretti demanded answers and transparency, saying they have been left in the dark for nine months while the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) have failed to provide any substantive update on the internal investigation. The couple’s outburst underscores growing public scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement tactics and raises questions about accountability mechanisms for law‑enforcement officers operating under the aegis of the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The incident that ignited the family’s crusade occurred on June 12, 2024, when a joint ICE‑CBP task force attempted to apprehend Alex Pretti, a 28‑year‑old undocumented immigrant who had been living in the Minneapolis metropolitan area for over a decade. According to court filings, agents fired a single shot that struck Pretti in the chest, killing him instantly. The agents involved were placed on administrative leave pending a “comprehensive review” by DHS, but no public findings have been released. The Prettis, who have been vocal advocates for immigration reform, say the lack of information suggests a deliberate effort to shield the officers from liability.

Legal experts point out that the federal government’s investigative process is governed by a complex web of statutes and internal policies, many of which are classified for security reasons. “While agencies do have the authority to conduct internal reviews, the public’s right to know, especially in a case that resulted in a death, is paramount,” said Professor Elena Ramirez, a constitutional law scholar at the University of Minnesota. “The absence of a transparent timeline or an independent oversight body fuels suspicion that the investigation is being managed to protect the agents rather than to uncover the truth.” Ramirez noted that similar cases—such as the 2022 shooting of a migrant worker in Arizona—have led to congressional hearings and calls for reform, but outcomes have often been limited to internal disciplinary actions that remain undisclosed.

The Prettis’ allegations come at a moment when the Biden administration is navigating a delicate balance between enforcing immigration laws and addressing humanitarian concerns. In recent months, DHS has faced criticism for a series of high‑profile incidents involving the use of lethal force, prompting calls from civil‑rights groups for stricter use‑of‑force protocols and greater civilian oversight. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request seeking all documents related to the Pretti shooting, arguing that the public interest outweighs any claimed need for secrecy.

Political reactions have been swift. Senator Amy Klobuchar (D‑MN) announced that her office will request a briefing from the DOJ on the status of the investigation, emphasizing that “the American people deserve clarity when a federal officer takes a life.” Conversely, Representative Jim Jordan (R‑OH) warned against what he described as “politicizing a tragic mistake,” urging the agencies to complete their internal review without external interference. The divergent viewpoints illustrate the broader partisan divide over immigration enforcement and federal accountability.

As the Pretti family continues to press for answers, they have pledged to pursue legal action if the government does not provide a full accounting. “We are not asking for sympathy; we are demanding justice for our son,” Michael Pretti said, his voice steady despite the emotion evident in his eyes. Their resolve reflects a growing trend of families seeking civil remedies when criminal prosecutions appear unlikely.

The coming weeks will likely determine whether the federal investigation proceeds in a manner that satisfies both legal standards and public expectations. If the DHS releases a detailed report or an independent body is appointed to review the case, it could set a precedent for handling similar incidents. Conversely, continued opacity may deepen mistrust in federal law‑enforcement agencies and intensify calls for legislative reforms aimed at increasing transparency and civilian oversight. For the Prettis, the pursuit of truth remains the only path toward closure, and the nation watches closely as the story unfolds.
